abstract: Conformal prediction ordinarily relies on exchangeable data and symmetric model fitting, conditions that can fail in ordered or drifting samples. We develop weighted split and full conformal procedures and a jackknife+ extension that accommodate departures from both assumptions. For full conformal prediction, prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] control residual quantiles, while fixed algorithm tags permit order-sensitive fitting. A weighted random swap, independent of the data, links miscoverage to the weighted mass of high-residual indices without requiring algorithmic symmetry. Finite-sample coverage is at least 1-alpha minus a weighted sum of total-variation distances between original and swapped residual distributions. This penalty vanishes for exchangeable data; under nonexchangeability, a small penalty limits undercoverage, and distinct residuals with small normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Simulations and electricity experiments show that calibration weighting can improve coverage at the cost of wider intervals, whereas weighted least squares can reduce width on ordered data. The randomly permuted electricity control shows no corresponding width advantage. Election experiments improve coverage but remain below the 90% target. The framework therefore connects validity to residual-distribution changes rather than promising nominal coverage under arbitrary drift.
methods: Theorem 2b fixes calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags t_i before observing the data. Normalize the weights together with a test weight of one, then draw K independently of the data with these probabilities. Fit the tagged algorithm after swapping observations K and n+1, leaving tags attached to their positions. At the true test label, let S(r) contain indices above the weighted (1-alpha)-quantile of a residual vector r; its total normalized weight is at most alpha. Because calibration weights cannot exceed the test weight, the quantile comparison implies that miscoverage requires K in S(R(Z^K)). Independence expresses this event's probability as a weighted sum over K. Comparing each swapped residual law with the original law adds at most its total-variation distance. The original-law contribution is at most alpha, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted swapped-residual penalty, without assuming symmetric fitting.
results: Table 2 separates calibration from fitting by comparing three full conformal procedures at a 90% target. On ordered electricity data, unweighted least squares (CP+LS) attains 85.2% coverage with mean width 0.565. Weighting calibration residuals alone (NexCP+LS) increases coverage to 89.0% but widens intervals to 0.606. Keeping residual weighting while using weighted least squares (NexCP+WLS) gives 89.3% coverage and width 0.527, showing that narrower intervals are not purchased through lower coverage. These are averages over prediction times, not uniformly valid coverage at each time. Under random permutation, which makes the sequence exchangeable, coverage is 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, respectively, while widths are 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. Thus the fitting change offers no width advantage in this control, and weighting adds variability. The ordered-data improvements support separate calibration and fitting roles in this setting; arbitrary drift can still produce a large swapped-residual total-variation penalty, so these observations do not establish universal 90% coverage.
notes: The WLS experiment description cites equation (14) rather than explicitly documenting the randomized swap in (20); confirm implementation before attributing empirical results to the theorem-guaranteed procedure. Table 2 gives temporal averages without uncertainty estimates; no significance claims or interval-width units were inferred. The residual total-variation penalty is not empirically quantified. Jackknife+ retains a 1-2alpha baseline guarantee, unlike split and full conformal. Near-nominal two-sided coverage additionally requires distinct residuals and a small normalized test weight.
